cards.#1: MacKenzie builds this one from retired sailcloth, so each bag carries the number of the sail it came from — 8185, in this case. Three were made, at $975. It is the piece people bring up when they talk about Sugarloaf, and the reason the waitlist exists at all.
cards.#2: White leather on a Double Seve body makes this the most expensive thing Sugarloaf has ever put its name on. MacKenzie builds the same 8-inch bag in canvas for $850, so the hide accounts for the rest of the $1400. White is a bold choice for something you carry across wet grass.
cards.#3: The standard-issue Double Seve carries the same 8-inch MacKenzie body, in canvas rather than white leather, and it sold at $850. That is the cheaper of the two by a wide margin, though $850 is still $850. Canvas will also scuff and soften in a way the white hide never would.
cards.#4: MacKenzie makes the shoe bag in navy canvas with the club crest on the face. It is one of the few pieces from the collaboration you can still buy, and at $195 it is the cheapest way into that work by a factor of four against the bags.
cards.#5: A navy, gold and white block stripe runs across the chest in the colours Sugarloaf drew up for TPC Sawgrass. It is an officially licensed PGA Tour product, which usually shows on the garment, and here the stripe carries the design instead of a logo. $95 for the polo.
cards.#6: The Caddie Crew comes in powder blue with the championship mark ringed on the chest. A ring reads collegiate rather than corporate, which is most of the difference between this and standard tournament merchandise. The colour helps too, since navy would have pushed it back towards a uniform.
cards.#7: The tech vest is black, quarter-zip and close to unbranded, which makes it the most wearable thing in the Sawgrass capsule. A vest with no visible tournament mark does not date the week it was made for. At $115 it goes over a polo in spring and under a shell later.
cards.#8: The Runner Cap is a nylon five-panel at $45, still in stock, and the easy way into the tournament work. Five-panel nylon sits flatter on the head than a structured crown, so it packs into a bag and comes back out fine. It is also the cheapest thing in the capsule by half.
cards.#9: Sugarloaf made this one with the Western Golf Association, in washed green with a flag at the chest pocket. The Evans Scholars program sends caddies to college on full housing-and-tuition scholarships, and the line supports it. At $44 it is the cheapest thing the two have done together, and the plainest.
cards.#10: A pistachio green pouch hangs off a plain webbing strap, and Sugarloaf shot it on a bag drop rather than a studio table. It is the accessory people ask about, which has more to do with the colour than the format. At $90 it was also one of the cheaper things in the scholarship work.
cards.#11: Sugarloaf made the Sport Polo with the Western Golf Association, and it is the piece from the scholarship run you can still buy at $95. The rest of that line sold through, so a polo is what remains of a collaboration built to put caddies through college on full housing and tuition.
cards.#12: Sugarloaf built a black carry bag for the Evans Scholars program and priced it at $375, which made it the most expensive piece in that line by a distance. A carry bag is the right object for the cause, given the program exists for people who walk the course with somebody else’s clubs.
cards.#13: Clubhaus is a Japanese golf media brand, and the capsule it made with Sugarloaf reads that way from the first piece. The headcover is navy knit with a multicolour tassel and a hedgehog at the crown, which is a more specific animal than most brands would land on. Sugarloaf priced it at $105.
cards.#14: A folding paper sensu fan, printed with the Clubhaus mark, sells for $14 and is the cheapest thing Sugarloaf has ever put its name on. It also explains the brand better than the bags do. The object is paper and one printed mark, and it exists because the collaboration was Japanese.
cards.#15: The windshirt is black, cropped and quarter-zip, which is about as much as a windshirt needs to be. Cropped is the part that dates it to this collaboration rather than to golf outerwear generally. It went in the first run at $125 and has not come back.
cards.#16: The valuables pouch is a zip pouch at $135, which is a Japanese-collaboration price if ever there was one. It holds what comes out of your pockets on the first tee and then goes back in the bag. Clubhaus put its mark on it and Sugarloaf sold it out.
cards.#17: PAYNTR builds the Eighty Seven and Sugarloaf did the colourway, which came out white with red detailing through the outsole. It landed in June 2026, timed to the U.S. Open, at $250. Red on a white shoe reads loud in a photograph and much quieter on a course.
cards.#18: The slides come in cream at $50, which puts them in the same drop as the shoe at a fifth of the price. They are made for the walk from the eighteenth to the car and nothing more demanding than that. PAYNTR built them; Sugarloaf picked the colour.
cards.#19: Sentinel makes everything in Japan and it shows in the hardware, which is the reason to look closely at what is otherwise a rangefinder case. This one is tan cordura with a blue stripe and a purple tab, three colours doing the job a logo does elsewhere, at $95.
cards.#20: The field jacket is red, sells at $355, and is the most substantial garment Sentinel and Sugarloaf have made together. A field jacket is a strange thing for a golf collaboration to land on, and a red one stranger still. It is also the only piece here you would wear off a course without thinking.
cards.#21: Students makes the polo in pale grey with a three-button placket and no visible branding beyond the collar. That is a hard thing to sell and an easy thing to wear, and it is the version of a collaboration polo that survives past the drop. $98, still in stock.
cards.#22: The Scout Hat is a white bucket with a scalloped brim and the Students wordmark on the front. A scalloped brim is the detail that separates it from every other white bucket hat on a course. It holds at $50 and is one of the few things here you can still order.
cards.#23: Don White ground clubs for tour players for decades, and these are his Boyd Blade and Ferrule Blade heads, done by hand and sold raw. Lofts run 24° through 47° with a slight square toe and a notch muscle, and raw means they arrive with oxidation and will rust unless you oil them. The set ships in a foam-lined flight case at $3000, the most serious object Sugarloaf has ever sold.
cards.#24: Makino mills the TOUR 3 and stamps the Sugarloaf arrow into the flange, which is the only branding on the club. Sugarloaf shot it on a park bench rather than a studio table, which tells you how the brand thinks about a $750 putter. There is an $800 version as well.
cards.#25: Bellroy is a leather-goods company out of Melbourne that had never made anything for golf before this. What it made was a cream ripstop sling at $90, which is the plainest possible answer to the brief. Ripstop keeps it light enough that you forget you are carrying it.
cards.#26: TOTEM makes the divot tool in brass, in three pieces, at $130. Brass is most of the appeal, because it darkens with handling rather than holding a finish, so the tool ages instead of wearing out. It is the nicest object Sugarloaf sells short of a bag.
cards.#27: Charlie makes the junior bag as a red, white and blue stand bag scaled for a kid, at $220, with a toddler version below it at $135. Very few brands build a proper stand bag at that size, and fewer still give one a real colourway rather than a cartoon.
cards.#28: The artist Gleezy drew a cartoon quail in golf shoes, and Sugarloaf put it on a $44 t-shirt for a Charlotte-specific run. A city graphic drawn by one artist is the kind of thing a brand does when it has no interest in selling the same shirt everywhere.
cards.#29: The same Charlotte run produced a headcover in purple and teal knit with a lilac tassel, at $95. It is the loudest thing Sugarloaf has made, and knit is the only construction that could carry those colours and the tassel without looking like a mistake.
cards.#30: Sugarloaf made a teal-striped soccer kit for Trellis Coffee Bar and sold it at $75 alongside golf bags. A golf brand producing a football shirt for a coffee shop is the clearest evidence that Sugarloaf works as a creative agency first and a golf label second.
cards.#31: The hoody costs $50 and comes out of a kids-and-parents capsule with Jain that also produced a Jainasaurus t-shirt and a Fore Ewe headcover. The name carries the whole idea, which is the adult version of what the kid is already wearing. It is one of the few things in the capsule still in stock.
cards.#32: The Tour Towel runs a teal stripe and holds at $95, which is a lot for a towel and about standard for this brand. Teal turns up across the stranger corners of the catalogue, and a towel is the easiest place to take it. Still in stock, which most of the archive is not.
cards.#33: The anorak is green terry cloth with a quarter-zip, at $165, and it sits in a full terry run that also takes in a cabana shirt, a short and a mini skirt. Terry is a pool fabric before it is a golf fabric, which is most of the reason it works here.
